title: Trace the user path, replication path, and recovery path
description: Switch scenarios to see which edges remain active. The modeled ledger changes by 180 GiB/day and normally replicates asynchronously, so the interconnect is off the user write path.

nodes.label: Users
nodes.detail: Users need a stable endpoint and a truthful result. Traffic steering can choose a healthy service, but it cannot decide which data copy is safe to promote.

nodes.label: Traffic director
nodes.detail: Applies health and recovery state to routing. It sends writes to the designated authority and changes targets only after the data promotion gate passes.

nodes.label: Primary API
nodes.detail: Owns the normal user path and writes only to the designated primary store. It emits stable operation identities so retries can be reconciled.

nodes.label: Recovery API
nodes.detail: Runs the same service contract but stays out of the write path until data, credentials, dependencies, and traffic controls are ready.

nodes.label: Primary store
nodes.detail: Protects order invariants and records the replication position. A timeout is reconciled here before a caller repeats a business operation.

nodes.label: Recovery store
nodes.detail: Applies the off-path change stream. Its last durable position defines the recovery point; copy existence alone does not prove promotability.

nodes.label: Orchestrator
nodes.detail: Reconciles desired placement and policy. Existing workloads should keep serving when it is unavailable, while new placement and rollout changes pause.

scenarios.label: Healthy
scenarios.summary: User writes stay inside Cloud A. Changed records move asynchronously to Cloud B at a modeled 180 GiB/day.
scenarios.result: The user path has no cross-cloud round trip. The recovery copy consumes outbound transfer and may lag, so monitoring must expose bytes sent, last applied position, age of the oldest unapplied record, and restore readiness.

scenarios.label: Interconnect down
scenarios.summary: Cloud A remains healthy, but the asynchronous replication link cannot reach Cloud B for two hours.
scenarios.result: Writes continue at the authority, but the recovery point ages and about 15 GiB of changed data accumulates at 180 GiB/day. When the link returns, catch-up traffic can exceed the normal egress rate; cap it so recovery does not saturate production.

scenarios.label: Primary cloud down
scenarios.summary: Cloud A and its store are unavailable. The recovery service is running, but traffic must wait for a safe data promotion decision.
scenarios.result: Resume writes only after verifying the last applied position, integrity, credentials, dependencies, and fencing of the old authority. The recovery point is bounded by replication lag; global routing alone cannot make a stale replica authoritative.

scenarios.label: Orchestrator down
scenarios.summary: The placement control plane is unavailable while both workload clusters and the replication path remain healthy.
scenarios.result: Existing data-plane workloads continue serving and replicating. New placements, policy changes, and automated recovery actions pause. This is why control-plane availability and workload availability need separate objectives and runbooks.

scenarios.label: WAN on write path
scenarios.summary: A design change requires Cloud B to acknowledge every write before Cloud A returns success.
scenarios.result: Each write now pays a cross-cloud round trip and outbound transfer. A link partition blocks safe writes in this two-site model: accepting on both sides risks divergence, while requiring both acknowledgements sacrifices write availability. Add a justified quorum design or keep WAN replication asynchronous.
